title: The AP quandary and how to resolve it
author: Chester E. Finn, Jr. and Michael J. Petrilli
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), November 5, 2026, November 6, 2026
summary: Chester Finn and Michael Petrilli examine the dilemma facing the College Board as the Advanced Placement program drifts from its gold-standard reputation. They lay out three pressures toward softening: passing an AP exam is meant to equal passing an introductory college course, and colleges now grade more generously; equity concerns, since poor and minority students enroll far more than they pass; and a shrinking high school population with dual enrollment and career pathways competing. They acknowledge the College Board has already changed how some exams are scored and has added subjects widely viewed as easier. Fordham, long an AP defender, accepts the reasons but regrets the result. Their proposal is transparency: count a 2 as passing for most colleges to reflect lower standards, while working with the most selective institutions to reserve credit for a 5, so the scale distinguishes performance again.
points: The AP exam's anchor, equivalence to an introductory college course, erodes when colleges inflate grades, so keeping the standard rigorous is structurally hard.
Equity pressure and the push for career-oriented subjects add incentives to widen access and ease the exams, and the College Board has already responded.
The authors call the board's position a quandary and avoid blaming it, noting that a nonprofit dependent on clients cannot easily resist the wider zeitgeist.
Their first recommendation is honest labelling: treat a 2 as passing for most colleges and urge states and nonselective universities to award credit.
Their second is to work with selective colleges so that a 5 earns genuine degree credit, restoring the top of the scale.
quotes: The Advanced Placement program is its biggest revenue generator and, along with the SAT, its showpiece. But where the SAT is little more than a measuring-and-comparison tool, the AP operation has long served as an indicator of educational quality and performance, often seen as the “gold standard” of high school achievement.

Should the Board make it harder to pass a college-level course than the colleges do? Bear in mind that 19 of its 31 trustees have day jobs in higher ed, often engaged in “enrollment management” for individual institutions.
But it’s also well known that poor and minority students are far likelier to enroll in AP courses than to pass AP exams.

So yes, the College Board has done some succumbing, most obviously by changing how student work on some of its most popular exams is evaluated, thereby boosting the shares of test-takers who pass and those who get high scores.

But is it realistic to expect a nonprofit organization—one that depends for its existence on clients and institutions that find it useful—to continue to resist changes in the zeitgeist that surrounds it?

We agree with some of the AP program’s critics that it’s a shame—and a problem for the country—that these widely respected tests appear to have gotten easier over time. As discussed above, we understand why that’s happened. And we understand that it’s hard to reverse, especially because it’s unclear what “standard” the AP should peg itself to, if not “a level of performance equivalent to passing an introductory college course.

First, in the interest of transparency, the College Board could declare that scores of 2 ought now to count as “passing” given the decline in college standards, making clear that this isn’t the Board’s preference but its acceptance of current reality, however regrettable.

In other words, the College Board should use the AP scoring system to differentiate the performance of students more clearly than today by acknowledging that a 2 indicates readiness to pass courses in most colleges in this time of grade inflation, while saving 5s for students at the very top of the performance distribution, making the Advanced Placement program at least 22-karat-gold-worthy again.
